findings.quote: taking rightward as positive for the first and leftward as positive for the second
findings.note: The text describes two different sign conventions, one per particle, but the equation on the same line uses a single axis (rightward positive) for both, which is what a dot product requires. If leftward were positive for the second particle its x-component would be +v₂, not −v₂, and the dot product −v₁v₂ + g²t² would not follow.
findings.fix: Write the velocity vectors of the two particles in one set of axes, rightward and upward positive; the first particle moves rightward and the second leftward.

findings.quote: Adding the speeds instead of multiplying them under the square root, using t = (v₁ + v₂)/g
findings.note: The cause is stated in a muddled way: 'adding under the square root' would give t = √7/g ≈ 0.26 s, while the formula actually named, t = (v₁ + v₂)/g, has no square root and does give 0.7 s. The numbers follow only from the formula, not from the wording.
findings.fix: Using t = (v₁ + v₂)/g in place of t = √(v₁v₂)/g gives a wrong time of 0.7 s and a wrong distance of 4.9 m (with g = 10 m/s²).

notes: Final answer and every equation line agree with my own solution. The vector line reuses the symbols v₁, v₂ both for the vectors and for the speeds, which the fix above also removes by naming the axes.
